declarations.description:
An alert that asks before something is done (UIAlertController's alert): a heading, a message, Cancel and the answer
that goes ahead. While `open` it is modal: the window behind it is dimmed and inert, the focus stays inside and goes
back where it was when the alert closes.

The answer that changes nothing is in front. With `destructive` the answer that goes ahead is red, and Cancel is
bold and has the focus, so a stray Return deletes nothing; without it the answer that goes ahead is bold and has the
focus.
Escape, and the browser's own request to close (a back gesture), answer Cancel. So does hiding what holds the alert
while it is open: a question nobody can see is not left over an inert page.

An answer closes the alert (`open` becomes false, the focus goes back) and then raises its event.

The two answers have the test ids `<data-testid of the alert>-cancel` and `<data-testid of the alert>-confirm`.

members.description: The browser asks to close a modal dialog (Escape, a back gesture): that is Cancel, and the alert closes itself.

members.name: onDialogClose
members.description:
The browser closed it without asking (it may, the second time it is asked in a row): still Cancel. `close` is told
late, so one from an answer already given can arrive after the alert was opened again: the dialog is open then, and
there is nothing to answer. Taken out of the page while open is not an answer either: it opens again when put back.

declarations.description:
A button in the four iOS styles. It is a real `<button>` inside, so Enter and Space press it, and it submits or
resets the form it sits in (`type`). A form control like the others (see `FormControl`): a disabled fieldset disables
it. A native submit button is the `submitter` of the `submit` event; a kit button cannot be, so `event.submitter` is
null and the form's data carries the button's `name` and `value` instead.

`fill` takes a data colour (a palette token such as `orange`, or `#rrggbb`) for a `filled` button; the text colour
is picked for 4.5:1 on it. Unlike `tint`, which is the control's accent, a fill is content.

Drawn 28 or 34 pt high. With `hit` it has a 44 x 44 pt hit area, as the shell's `hit` does (see `FormControl`).

declarations.description:
A picker (SwiftUI's `Picker` in its menu style, a pop-up button): one choice from a list too long, or too changeable,
for a `ui-segmented`. It shows the chosen option and opens the system's own menu of them, so the keyboard, type-ahead
and a screen reader work as they do on every select. A form control (see `FormControl`): the chosen value is
submitted, and `required` keeps the form invalid until an option is chosen.

With a `value` no option has, it shows nothing chosen. Drawn 36 pt high inside a 44 pt high target, all
of which opens the menu.

declarations.description:
One row of a `ui-list` (UITableViewCell): a title and subtitle, an optional icon tile, a value, a chevron, and
slots for anything else.

A row is plain text until it is `tappable`. A tappable row has one tab stop and fires `press` when it is tapped; the
content in its `trailing` slot (a `ui-toggle`, a button) stays separately clickable and does not press the row. In a
list with `selection`, a row is an option: it shows `selected`, and a tap, Enter or Space fires `press`.

Listen for `press`, not `click`: a `click` bubbles from everything inside the row, a flipped trailing toggle included.

`insetGrouped` block of iPadOS Settings.

A form is a section of rows with a field each, and its footer is where the form speaks: a note on what the fields
are for, or, with `footer-tone="error"`, what is wrong with what was typed (red, and announced when it appears).

declarations.description:
A segmented control (UISegmented Control): one choice from a few. A radio group: Tab reaches the selected segment,
the arrow keys move the selection, Home and End jump. A form control (see `FormControl`): the selected value is
submitted, and `required` keeps the form invalid until a segment is chosen.

Each segment has the test id `<data-testid of the control>-<value>`. The segments are drawn 28 pt high inside a
44 pt high hit area.

declarations.description:
A sidebar beside a detail (UISplitViewController, SwiftUI's `NavigationSplitView`), with a `content` column between
them when one is slotted. Given 700 pt or more it shows every column; given less it is `collapsed` and shows one:
the one `column` names (`NavigationSplitView`'s `preferredCompactColumn`). The app sets `column` as the person goes
in (they picked a row: `detail`) and back out.

The way back is the app's, in the header of what it shows, as a navigation bar's back button is: draw it while the
split view is `collapsed`, and set `column` when it is pressed. Read `collapsed`, or hear `collapsedchange`, for that
and for whether a selection is worth showing in the sidebar (collapsed, the sidebar is a list to pick from).

When the column in front changes while the keyboard is in the one that goes, the focus moves to the column that
comes, as iPadOS moves it into the view that was pushed: Tab goes on from there, and a screen reader keeps its place.
The column's element takes it, and is given `tabindex="-1"` for that, which it keeps (no ring is drawn around it).

It fills the height its parent gives it, and each column gives its one element its whole box.
declarations.name: UiSplitView

declarations.description:
A multi-line text field (UITextView, SwiftUI's `TextEditor`): what `ui-text-field` is for one line, for many. Return
starts a new line and never submits the form. A form control (see `FormControl`): with a `name` it submits its text,
and `required`, the length limits and `setCustomValidity` take part in validation.

It is `rows` lines high (with `hit`, never under 44 pt) and scrolls in itself past that; given a height by its
parent (a flex or grid item, a `height`), it fills it. There is no resize handle, as there is none on iPadOS.

declarations.description:
A single-line text field that takes what an ordinary text input takes: `type` (including `number`), `inputmode`,
`maxlength`, `minlength`, `pattern`, `min`, `max`, `step`, `enterkeyhint`, `autocapitalize`, `autocomplete`. A form
control (see `FormControl`): with a `name` it submits its value, Enter submits the form, and `required`, the length and
pattern limits and `setCustomValidity` take part in validation (`checkValidity`, `validity`, ...).

The field is drawn 36 pt high inside a 44 pt high hit area (a click on the strip around it focuses it).

declarations.description:
What `ui-toggle` and `ui-check` share: an on/off value that takes part in a form (see `FormControl`) and says so with
`change`. While on it submits `value`; `required` keeps the form invalid until it is on (the "I agree" check).

The control inside is a real `<button role=...>`, so it has focus, Space and Enter for free. A click on a
`<label for>` reaches the host, not that button, so the host toggles for a click that did not start inside.

members.name: hit
members.description:
A 44 x 44 pt hit area around the drawn control, as the shell's `hit` is (off by default: the control is drawn at its
own size). Set it wherever nothing else gives the control a 44 pt target; a row, a banner and a toolbar item do.

members.name: label

members.description: Read after the name.

members.name: validationAnchor
members.description: The element in the shadow root the browser points at when it reports a problem.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control takes no input: itself disabled, or inside a disabled fieldset. One answer, the browser's own
(`:disabled` is true for the `disabled` attribute and for a disabled ancestor fieldset), so the two cannot disagree.
`willUpdate` keeps the attribute in step with the property before the render that reads this.

members.description: The accessible name: `label`, else the text of the first `<label>` that names this element.

members.description: The form the control is in, or null.

members.name: labels
members.description: The `<label>` elements that name the control.

members.name: setCustomValidity
members.description: Marks the control invalid with a message of the app's own (`''` clears it), as a native input does.

members.name: swallowWhenDisabled
members.description: A native disabled control hears no click: `el.click()` on a disabled kit control reaches nobody either.

members.name: syncForm
members.description: Tells the form the current value and validity.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The element's own attribute or a fieldset turned it on or off: draw again (`isDisabled` reads the browser).
